thread.title: Senators introduce Tibet Atrocities Determination Act requiring State Department review
thread.title_full: Senators introduce Tibet Atrocities Determination Act requiring State Department review

author: Sunshine Sentinel
title: Senators introduce Tibet Atrocities Determination Act requiring State Department review
text:
Senator Rick Scott and Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the Tibet Atrocities Determination Act on April 29, a date observed by the Tibetan Youth Congress as Martyr’s Day to honor Tibetans who have lost their lives for the freedom of Tibet. The proposed legislation would require the Secretary of State to formally determine whether China is committing genocide or crimes against humanity against the Tibetan people.
The issue addresses ongoing concerns about human rights in Tibet and seeks to hold China accountable for alleged abuses. The bill comes amid longstanding reports of cultural suppression, forced displacement, and other forms of repression faced by Tibetans under Chinese rule.
Scott said, “Communist China is committing genocide in Tibet. There is no way around it. The regime in Beijing has engaged in systematic killings, torture, forced sterilization, forced displacement, government sanctioned kidnapping, and a myriad of other crimes against humanity in its oppression of the Tibetan people. This is par for the course for an evil regime that is simultaneously waging a genocide against the Uyghurs, suppressing Christianity, and locking up political prisoners like my friend Jimmy Lai. The bloodshed needs to end, and China needs to be held accountable for all of it.
I am glad to be partnering with Sen. Merkley on this effort to hold the Chinese government accountable.”
Merkley said, “In the face of China’s continued assault on Tibetans—escalating cultural erasure, child separation, surveillance, imprisonment, and torture—America can’t stand silent As the Chinese government continues to ignore the rights of the Tibetan people under international law, we must be clear that these crimes will not be ignored.”
After China’s 1949 revolution led by the Communist Party (CCP), authorities moved into Tibet in 1950 with military force and established control through agreements such as the Seventeen Point Agreement signed in 1951. According to historical accounts included in legislative background materials provided by Scott’s office (see official press release), this ended Tibetan self-rule and resulted in events such as mass arrests during uprisings like Lhasa’s in 1959. In subsequent decades there have been restrictions on religion and culture including regulation or closure of monasteries; punishment for support shown toward figures like Dalai Lama; enforced disappearances; arbitrary detention; reported torture; unresolved cases such as that involving Panchen Lama since his disappearance in 1995; as well as allegations regarding boarding schools separating children from families while limiting language instruction—all documented by U.S. State Department reports.
Scott champions fiscal responsibility along with debt reduction policies supporting families and small businesses according to his official website. He served on active duty aboard USS Glover after high school according to his official website. Scott won election representing Florida according to his official website, holds degrees from University of Missouri-Kansas City (business) and Southern Methodist University (law) according to his official website, serves on Senate Committees including Armed Services among others according to his official website, and together with wife Ann raised two daughters according to his official website.
The introduction of this bill reflects growing calls within Congress for greater scrutiny over China’s actions regarding ethnic minorities within its borders.
